title.undergrad: What a brain tumour looks like on MRI
title.med: Glioma on MRI: enhancement, core and edema

summary.undergrad: This is a research scan of a person with a [[glioma]], a tumour that grows from the brain's own supporting cells. Pane A is T1 after a [[gadolinium]] injection (T1 +C); pane B is [[flair|FLAIR]]. The coloured outline was drawn by experts for the dataset: blue where the tumour takes up contrast, red for the tumour's inner part that does not, and yellow for the swollen tissue around it ([[edema]]). Use the switches to hide the outline and look at the image underneath, and turn the 3D view to see the tumour inside the brain.
summary.med: A research case from the Medical Segmentation Decathlon brain tumour set (BraTS-derived [[glioma]] data). Pane A is post-[[gadolinium]] T1 (T1 +C), pane B is [[flair|FLAIR]]. The expert labels mark three compartments: [[enhancement|enhancing]] tumour (blue), non-enhancing tumour core including [[necrosis]] (red), and peritumoral FLAIR hyperintensity, labelled [[edema]] (yellow). Study how each compartment looks on each sequence, then hide the labels and find the boundaries yourself. The text describes these appearances in general; it gives no diagnosis or grade for this person.

source.text: Medical Segmentation Decathlon, brain tumour case BRATS_449 (Simpson et al. 2019)

text.undergrad: The bright ring on T1 +C (A). The contrast agent normally stays inside blood vessels; here it leaks out into the tumour, so the tumour's living edge lights up.
text.med: Thick, irregular [[enhancement]] on T1 +C (A): gadolinium crosses a disrupted blood–brain barrier in viable tumour. Note the ring shape around a non-enhancing centre.

text.undergrad: Inside the ring the tumour stays dark on T1 +C (A). This part takes up no contrast; in tumours like this it often contains dead tissue.
text.med: Central non-enhancing component, hypointense on T1 +C. In general, a non-enhancing centre within an enhancing ring often corresponds to [[necrosis]]; the label groups it with non-enhancing tumour.

text.undergrad: Bright on FLAIR (B) but not bright on T1 +C (A). This is extra water in the brain tissue around the tumour ([[edema]]).
text.med: Peritumoral FLAIR hyperintensity (B) without enhancement (A), labelled edema. In general it is vasogenic edema and may also contain non-enhancing infiltrating tumour, which MRI cannot separate reliably.

landmarks.name: Fluid in a ventricle, for comparison

text.undergrad: Normal brain fluid (CSF): dark on both. Compare it with the tumour's centre and the swelling, which are not simply fluid.
text.med: CSF in the lateral [[ventricle]]: hypointense on T1 +C and nulled on FLAIR. A space-occupying lesion can compress or displace nearby ventricles ([[mass-effect|mass effect]]); compare both sides of this slice.

prompt.undergrad: The marker is on the bright ring in pane A (T1 after contrast). Why is the ring bright?
prompt.med: The marker is on the enhancing rim. What does gadolinium enhancement in brain tissue indicate, in general?

options: Contrast agent leaks out of damaged blood vessels into the tissue
The ring is made of fat

explanation.undergrad: Healthy brain vessels keep the contrast agent in (the blood–brain barrier). Where a tumour damages them, it leaks out and the tissue turns bright.
explanation.med: Enhancement reflects contrast leaving the vessels where the blood–brain barrier is disrupted, as in viable high-cellularity tumour; it is not specific to tumour.

prompt.undergrad: The marker is in the swelling around the tumour. Which pane shows it as bright?
prompt.med: Which sequence best shows the extent of the peritumoral signal change at the marker?

options: Neither: it looks normal on both

explanation.undergrad: Edema is extra water in the tissue. FLAIR shows water in tissue as bright while switching off the free fluid in the ventricles.
explanation.med: FLAIR suppresses CSF but keeps T2 contrast, so increased tissue water (edema, infiltrative tumour) stands out; it does not enhance on T1 +C.

prompt.med: The marker is in the centre of the ring. What does a non-enhancing centre inside an enhancing ring often correspond to, in general?

explanation.med: A central non-enhancing area within a thick irregular enhancing rim commonly represents necrosis; the appearance alone is not diagnostic.
